DKnown-Jev-2: Article-Level Answer-Evidence Classification and Efficient Inference with a Pre-trained Language Model

Qi Li ††thanks: Contact: liqi@czkj1010.com.    Jianjun Xu    Jiu Li    Pingtao Wei Affiliation: Beijing Caizhi Tech, Beijing, China

Abstract

Evidence selection in normative knowledge question answering requires determining whether a candidate article contains content that directly supports an answer under the applicable conditions of the question. We present DKnown-Jev-2, an article-level answer evidence classifier designed for evidence integration across multiple paragraphs. The model jointly encodes question conditions, article metadata, and paragraph content, and uses a pointer-style classification head to predict Answer Evidence (AE) and Non-answer Evidence (NE) in a single forward pass. On a manually annotated test set of 972 evaluation instances, DKnown-Jev-2 achieves 91.77% accuracy and 91.28% macro-F1, outperforming Jev by 2.16 and 2.37 percentage points, respectively, while reducing both evidence misses and non-evidence false positives. The test set contains 317 multi-paragraph instances, with a maximum body length of 9,322 characters. Shared article encoding and non-autoregressive classification support low-latency inference. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for article-level evidence selection in normative knowledge question answering.

Keywords: pre-trained language model; article-level evidence classification; domain adaptation; pointer network; long-context processing; inference efficiency

1 Introduction

In normative knowledge applications, determining whether a candidate text provides an answer or part of an answer is different from measuring semantic relevance to the question. Normative knowledge is issued, maintained, or published by a responsible authority, and its applicability depends on the subject, time, version, and other scope conditions. A candidate text contributes evidence only when it is valid under those conditions and provides an explicit basis for the requested matter. Evidence selection therefore requires joint reasoning over question conditions, article attributes, and textual content.

Candidate articles in practical systems commonly contain metadata and multiple body paragraphs. Different paragraphs may jointly provide eligibility, required materials, and procedural information, while also containing tables of contents, duplicated text, or background explanations. Compared with the single-paragraph data used in prior work, the article-level data considered here requires extracting evidence from longer text, integrating multiple paragraphs, and distinguishing complete answers, partial answers, and background information.

We formulate article-level answer evidence identification as a binary classification task over a user question, its applicable conditions, and a candidate article. AE includes a complete answer or an explicit answer component; NE includes contextual material, inapplicable content, and material without substantive relevance. Each prediction analyzes all paragraphs in the input article.

Prior DKnown-Jev combines question conditions, article metadata, and a single candidate paragraph under the same AE/NE label semantics [1]. This work extends the prediction unit to all paragraphs belonging to one article and evaluates article-level classification on 972 instances. We study overall classification performance and performance stratified by the number of input paragraphs.

2 Related Work

Retrieval-augmented generation uses external material to support knowledge-intensive tasks [2]. Dense retrieval and cross-encoder reranking provide complementary mechanisms for candidate recall and relevance assessment [3,4]. Our task uses answer-support relations and applicability conditions as the classification criteria.

Natural-language label definitions can participate in classification decisions, while textual-entailment classification and text-to-text learning provide related modeling perspectives [5,6]. We describe AE and NE with natural-language definitions and determine the label from matching scores between candidate representations and a decision representation. Parameter-efficient adaptation methods such as LoRA provide a practical route for domain adaptation [7].

3 Task Definition and Label Semantics

3.1 Input Representation and Classification Objective

Each instance is represented as x=(q,c,a,P)x=(q,c,a,P), where qq is the user question, cc contains available conditions such as the service region and consultation date, aa contains article attributes such as title, region, and publication date, and P=(p1,l​d​o​t​s,pm)P=(p_{1},ldots,p_{m}) is the ordered sequence of input paragraphs. The model estimates pθ​(y|x)p_{\theta}(y|x), where y∈{AE,NE}y\in\{\mathrm{AE},\mathrm{NE}\}. The predicted label is y^=arg⁡maxy​pθ​(y|x)\hat{y}=\arg\max_{y}p_{\theta}(y|x).

The same article can receive different labels for different questions. Classification must jointly inspect paragraph content and article metadata to verify the applicable region, time, subject, and scope of the rule.

3.2 Label Definitions and Decision Criteria

A partial answer may provide an applicable definition, rule, condition, material requirement, procedure, or concrete fact; the article need not answer every aspect of the question. Related material may aid background understanding without supplying answer content. A rule that does not apply to the user and cannot support any answer component is NE.

For example, consider the question: “What conditions and materials are required for free repair of a Model A device?” A Model B repair policy cannot serve as evidence for Model A even if the wording is highly similar. The current Model A policy “A manufacturing defect occurring during the warranty period is eligible for free repair” answers the condition component and is therefore a partial answer. A valid supplementary document stating “the purchase receipt must be attached” provides another answer component. A paragraph that merely describes after-sales-service principles is relevant background, not a procedural basis. These cases illustrate the distinction between inapplicable content, partial answers, and contextual references.

The decision uses both paragraph content and article metadata to distinguish complete answers, partial answers, contextual references, and inapplicable content, then maps them to AE or NE. Multiple paragraphs may jointly support an answer. The labels encode applicability and answer contribution under the given conditions; they are not thresholded semantic-similarity scores.

3.3 Model Output

The model outputs a probability distribution over AE and NE together with a predicted label. Metrics are computed against the manually assigned label. In downstream answer generation, completeness, evidence conflicts, and citation support must still be checked. When scope information is insufficient to establish applicability, an application may retain an unresolved status and verify it after additional scope information is obtained; this status is not an additional label in the binary evaluation.

4 Dataset and Evaluation Protocol

4.1 Dataset Size and Class Distribution

The test set contains 972 manually annotated evaluation instances. Each instance consists of a user question, applicable conditions, a candidate article, and its label. Article body length is computed as the sum of the character counts of all input paragraphs.

Because NE accounts for 62.76% of the test set, an always-NE majority baseline has 62.76% accuracy. Macro-F1 and per-class metrics are also reported to evaluate both labels.

4.2 Input Alignment and Evaluation Integrity

We compare DKnown-Jev-2 with Jev and OpenAI Decision. OpenAI Decision denotes the decision service accessed through the OpenAI Decisions API [8], which selects from predefined candidates and returns a probability distribution. All three systems predict the same 972 test instances, yielding 2,916 predictions. Predictions are aligned by question, applicable conditions, and article content; each instance has one reference label and three model predictions.

4.3 Task Complexity and Multi-paragraph Long-context Inputs

The dataset is substantially more demanding than the prior single-paragraph setting. Its difficulty arises from evidence identification under applicability constraints: users may ask about several matters at once, answer clues may be distributed across paragraphs, and valid evidence may be interleaved with tables of contents, duplicated text, and incomplete sentences. The model must locate and integrate answer components in longer text and then verify applicability using regional, temporal, and article metadata.

Multi-paragraph inputs account for 32.61% of the test set, including 12.96% with at least four paragraphs. These inputs require joint reasoning over multiple paragraphs to determine whether the article provides applicable answer evidence.

5 Model Architecture and Inference Mechanism

5.1 Backbone and Input Organization

DKnown-Jev-2 is built on Qwen3.5-9B [9] and uses a pointer-style decision structure. Hidden states at candidate markers and a decision marker are used by the pointer head to compute AE/NE scores. The input contains the question and conditions, article metadata, paragraph sequence, a classification instruction, and natural-language definitions of AE and NE. A candidate marker terminates each candidate definition, and a decision marker terminates the input sequence. Paragraphs are serialized in order with their title and body; article attributes are shared context. Marker indices are recorded during tokenization to locate the final hidden states.

5.2 Pointer-style Classification Head

Pointer Networks associate predictions with input positions through attention scores [10]. We adopt this position-selection idea by extracting a representation at each candidate marker and matching it with the decision representation. Let hkh_{k} be the final hidden state at candidate marker kk and hd​e​ch_{dec} the state at the decision marker:

ck=Wc​LN​(hk),r=Wq​LN​(hd​e​c).c_{k}=W_{c}\mathrm{LN}(h_{k}),\hskip 20.00003ptr=W_{q}\mathrm{LN}(h_{dec}).

With projection dimension d=256d=256, the score is

zk=ck⊤​rd+w⊤​ck.z_{k}=\frac{c_{k}^{\top}r}{\sqrt{d}}+w^{\top}c_{k}.

Here Wc,Wq∈ℝd×HW_{c},W_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times H} are trainable projections, HH is the backbone hidden size, and w∈ℝdw\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is trainable. Scores are normalized as

pk=exp⁡(zk/τ)∑jexp⁡(zj/τ),k,j∈{AE,NE},p_{k}=\frac{\exp(z_{k}/\tau)}{\sum_{j}\exp(z_{j}/\tau)},\hskip 10.00002ptk,j\in\{\mathrm{AE},\mathrm{NE}\},

where τ>0\tau>0 is a temperature parameter. The prediction is y^=arg⁡maxk⁡pk\hat{y}=\arg\max_{k}p_{k}. Both labels share the backbone and classification head; their semantics are supplied through the natural-language definitions.

5.3 Hybrid Attention and Cross-paragraph Interaction

In full-attention layers, the region from the beginning of the decision context to the last decision marker is bidirectionally visible, allowing candidate representations to use article context and compare candidates. Linear-attention layers remain causal. The two attention mechanisms jointly process question conditions, article paragraphs, and candidate definitions. Consistent visibility rules are used during training and inference, allowing candidate and decision representations to integrate evidence distributed across paragraphs.

5.4 Training Objective and Domain Adaptation

Domain adaptation uses supervised training instances labeled AE or NE. The pointer head outputs a binary probability distribution, and the one-hot reference label is represented by target vector tt. The basic objective is cross-entropy:

LC​E=−∑ktklogpk.L_{CE}=-\sum_{k}t_{k}\log p_{k}.

The training framework also supports an RLCD auxiliary objective that perturbs class scores and optimizes probability-distribution scores. When enabled, the total objective is L=LC​E+λ​LR​L​C​DL=L_{CE}+\lambda L_{RLCD}, where λ\lambda is the auxiliary-loss weight. We do not attribute performance gains to RLCD alone.

5.5 Non-autoregressive Classification Inference

Inference constructs the input sequence, records marker positions, performs one backbone forward pass, extracts candidate and decision representations, and normalizes classification scores. AE and NE scores are produced simultaneously and converted with Softmax into a probability distribution; the maximum-probability label is returned without autoregressive decoding. Compared with the predecessor’s separate article encoding for each candidate, organizing the article and all candidate definitions in one sequence reduces repeated encoding and token-by-token decoding overhead.

6 Experimental Setup

6.1 Baselines and Evaluation Principles

We evaluate DKnown-Jev-2 against Jev and OpenAI Decision on the same test set. All systems use the same AE/NE semantics and the same manually annotated reference labels.

6.2 Metrics

We report Accuracy, Macro-F1, class precision, and class recall. AE is the positive class; an NE instance predicted as AE is a false positive (FP), while an AE instance predicted as NE is a false negative (FN). T​PTP and T​NTN denote correctly identified AE and NE instances, and NN is the total number of instances.

A​c​c​u​r​a​c​y=T​P+T​NN,P​r​e​c​i​s​i​o​n=T​PT​P+F​P,R​e​c​a​l​l=T​PT​P+F​N.Accuracy=\frac{TP+TN}{N},\hskip 10.00002ptPrecision=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\hskip 10.00002ptRecall=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}.
F​1=2​T​P2​T​P+F​P+F​N.F1=\frac{2TP}{2TP+FP+FN}.

Macro-F1 is the arithmetic mean of the AE and NE F1 scores. Error counts and class metrics are used to analyze evidence misses and non-evidence false positives.

7 Results

7.1 Classification Performance

DKnown-Jev-2 outperforms both baselines on all reported classification metrics. Compared with Jev, it improves accuracy and Macro-F1 by 2.16 and 2.37 percentage points, respectively, adds 21 correctly classified instances, and reduces false negatives by 17 and false positives by 4. This indicates higher AE recall while preserving AE precision.

7.2 Complex Article Scenarios

We stratify the test set into single-paragraph, 2–3 paragraph, and 4-or-more-paragraph groups.

DKnown-Jev-2 has the highest accuracy in all three groups, reaching 92.67% and 92.06% in the 2–3 and 4-or-more paragraph groups. The grouping is based on paragraph count; performance is also affected by question content, class distribution, and applicability conditions.

In the inference benchmark, on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 with 24 GB of VRAM, the model has an average response time of approximately 118 ms with concurrency set to one, providing low-latency evidence selection.

8 Conclusion

We presented DKnown-Jev-2, an article-level answer evidence classifier that jointly incorporates question conditions, article metadata, and multiple paragraphs, and performs non-autoregressive classification with a pointer-style head. The method shifts evidence selection from topical relevance toward answer support under explicit applicability conditions and extends the prediction unit from a single paragraph to an article’s paragraph sequence. Experiments show improved evidence recognition in complex article scenarios. Shared article encoding and non-autoregressive classification reduce repeated computation and provide a practical path to low-latency evidence selection. The model can serve as an evidence-selection component in retrieval-augmented generation by determining whether a candidate article supports an answer under the given conditions.
